title: Eid al-Adha
hookLine: the feast of sacrifice remembers Ibrahim, and the meat is shared in thirds

cards: A freezer after a family celebration: foil packets, labeled in marker, stacked up, some already promised to other people. In some Muslim homes, the day after Arafah ends like that.
It starts with the Eid prayer, early, in new or best clothes. Hugs, and eid mubarak again. Then a very old question: who gets the meat?
This is the second of the two Eids, and the end of a run on this path that began with a new moon.

teach.b: Eid al-Adha means the feast of the sacrifice. It falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the day after Arafah, while the pilgrims are finishing the Hajj. It remembers a story in Surah as-Saffat.

teach.h: IBRAHIM, HIS SON, AND A RANSOM.
teach.b: Ibrahim sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son, and tells him. The son answers: do what you are commanded; you'll find me, if Allah wills, among the patient. They both submit.
Then Allah calls out to Ibrahim that he has already fulfilled the vision, and verse one hundred seven says: Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim. The Qur'an doesn't name the son here.
Tradition usually names Isma'il; some early scholars said Ishaq. Either way, the story ends with a life spared.
In South Asia and elsewhere, the sacrifice is called qurbani, from the Arabic qurban, from a root meaning to be near: an offering is a way of drawing near. In Arabic it's usually called udhiyah.
Families who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, a goat, or a share in a cow or camel, or pay someone to do it for them, often in a poorer country.
Scholars differ on how binding it is: the Hanafi school calls it required for those who can afford it; the other major schools call it a strongly recommended sunnah.
The Qur'an, in Surah al-Hajj, says the flesh and the blood don't reach Allah; what reaches Him is your devotion. So the meat is for people.
The same surah says to eat of it and feed the poor, and a common recommendation divides it in three: a third for the household, a third for relatives and friends, a third for the poor.
A feast that isn't finished until someone who has nothing gets a plate.

how: On the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah Muslims pray the Eid prayer, and families who can afford it sacrifice an animal, often dividing the meat among the household, relatives and friends, and the poor.

games.why: the son accepts, and at the last moment Allah ransoms him with a tremendous sacrifice (37:102–107). the story ends with a life spared.

practice: Picture your next meal and divide it in your mind: one part for your household, one for someone you know, a friend, a neighbor, a relative you haven't called, and one for someone you don't know who needs it.
Watch each plate go to its place.

wordCard.voice: Qurbani. The sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, from a root meaning to be near, its meat shared with family, friends and the poor. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: an offering, from the root q-r-b, to be near. 'qurbani' is the Urdu and Persian form.
